title: What are professional services firms actually using AI for?
description: Where AI pays first at engineering, architecture, consulting, agency and IT firms of 40-500 staff. What a saved hour is worth, and who signs off.
verdict: Professional services firms are among the heaviest AI users: 39.1% in mid-2026, against 21.5% of all businesses.[^1][^2]
The main uses are research, summaries, meeting notes and proposals: drafting work a professional reviews before it goes out.[^3][^4]
Time saved rarely becomes revenue: in a vendor survey of services firms, 84.8% save time but 29.9% earn more.[^5][^3]
On hourly contracts a saved hour shrinks the bill unless resold; on fixed fees it becomes margin or capacity.[^6][^7]
Licensed engineers keep the seal: boards say they must check, document and be able to reproduce AI output.[^8][^9]

answers.human-role: Your professionals stay in charge of every judgment and signature: AI drafts, and the licensee, engagement lead or recruiter decides.[^8][^10]
answers.ranked: AI pays first on the unbilled writing around client work: proposals, notes and status reports, then research summaries and time capture.[^11][^4]
answers.rules: Professional licensing rules bind engineers and architects, hiring-AI laws bind anyone screening candidates, and federal rules cover fake reviews and copyright.[^8][^12]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI goes wrong when unchecked output reaches a client: invented citations, wrong answers on hard tasks, and sloppy drafts colleagues must fix.[^13][^14]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when software you already own does the job, or when the contract, not the tool, is the problem.[^15][^16]

summary: AI for professional services firms means tools that draft, summarize and search the written work that fills a professional's week.[^3][^4] It makes people faster and better on tasks it handles well, and worse on others.[^14][^17] Whether saved hours become revenue decides the payoff.[^5]
humanRole: Licensed engineers keep responsible charge: the engineering licensing council (NCEES) says they validate AI output and document methods.[^8][^9] American Institute of Architects (AIA) Rule 4.102 bars sealing documents not prepared under your responsible control.[^10]

The engagement lead, partner or principal reviews every client-facing output before it leaves.[^14] AI-invented citations reached government clients in published cases in Australia and Canada.[^13][^18]
Your COO or managing partner decides where saved hours go: resold, moved to fixed fee or passed on.[^16][^7] Only 29.9% of firms say AI raises revenue so far (vendor-sponsored survey).[^5]
Recruiters keep the shortlist and the hiring call.[^19] Illinois requires notice when AI is used in employment decisions, and NYC requires a bias audit first.[^12][^20]

ranked.name: Proposals and request for proposal (RFP) responses
ranked.why: Proposals eat unbilled senior time, and Bentley found proposal-style work in AI production at 86.4% of 103 design and engineering firms.[^11][^21] A Loopio vendor survey puts one RFP at 25 hours, down from 30.[^22]
ranked.payoff: Senior hours per proposal, and win rate, before and after.

ranked.name: Meeting notes, status reports and client updates
ranked.why: In a vendor-sponsored survey of professional services leaders, 28% of client-facing staff spend more than 30% of their week on admin.[^23] Among US agencies, 74% already use AI to summarize documents.[^4]
ranked.payoff: Minutes per status report, and the edits the engagement lead makes before sending.

ranked.name: Research and document summaries
ranked.why: In a field study of 758 consultants, AI users finished 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, on tasks AI handles well.[^14][^24] Professionals took 40% less time on writing tasks in a Science study.[^17]
ranked.payoff: Hours from question to checked summary, with every source verified by a person.

ranked.name: Time capture, timesheets and invoicing
ranked.why: Missed time is lost revenue on hourly work, and 44% of professionals in a vendor survey lose 4+ hours a week to admin.[^25][^23] Productive fills timesheets from calendar events, and BigTime sells an AI assistant (vendor features).[^26][^15]
ranked.payoff: Hours logged per person each week, and time written off at billing.

ranked.name: Searching firm knowledge: past proposals, specs and deliverables
ranked.why: Every firm holds years of past work that is hard to find, and engineering firms name data quality as the first barrier to AI.[^27][^11] We found no sound payoff figure, so measure your own.
ranked.payoff: Minutes to find a past proposal or spec, sampled before and after.

ranked.name: First drafts of routine reports, specs, briefs and code
ranked.why: At Procter & Gamble, one professional with AI matched a two-person team without it.[^28] Developers with AI completed 26.08% more tasks; a 2025 trial found experienced developers slower, but its authors now think they are likely faster.[^29][^30]
ranked.payoff: Reviewer edit time per draft, and defects found after delivery.

ranked.name: Staffing and search: screening and interview scheduling
ranked.why: In Bullhorn's vendor survey of recruitment professionals, 46% of firms say AI halved screening time, but only 10% use agentic AI across the full workflow.[^19] Hiring-AI laws apply, so read the rules below first.[^12][^20]
ranked.payoff: Days from job order to shortlist, with each adverse-impact check logged.

ownData.title: What is one hour a week worth at a 100-person firm?
ownData.intro: By our math, one hour a week per person at a 100-person firm is $573,000-$700,000 of hourly revenue, or $219,000-$272,000 of payroll on fixed fees.[^6] The inputs are receipts, payroll and staff from the Census Bureau's 2022 Economic Census, for firms with 50-499 staff, pulled 26 Nov 2026.[^6][^31] Method: receipts and payroll per employee, divided by a 2,000-hour year, times 5,000 hours (100 people, one hour, 50 weeks).[^32]
headers: Hourly work: revenue at stake a year (our math)
Fixed fee: payroll freed a year (our math)
rows: IT services and computer systems design (5415)
ownData.note: Limits: 2022 figures, not inflation-adjusted, counting all staff, so revenue per billable hour runs higher; payroll excludes benefits and payroll taxes.[^6] Agency receipts can include pass-through media billings, and averages hide a wide spread between firms. Staffing firms are left out because placed workers on their payroll distort these figures.

tables.title: Where does a saved hour go under each kind of contract?
tables.intro: A saved hour goes to the client on hourly work and to the firm on fixed-fee work, unless you change the contract.[^7][^16] Hourly billing is sticky: 78% of tax firms still bill by the hour.[^16]

rows.name: Time and materials (hourly)
cells: To the client, as a smaller bill, unless the hour is resold[^6]
Resell freed hours, or move suitable scopes to fixed fee[^7]

rows.name: Fixed fee or lump sum
cells: To the firm, as margin or capacity[^6]
Keep the review time inside the fee

rows.name: Retainer
cells: To the firm until renewal, when the client may ask for a share[^35]
Show the added value at renewal

rows.name: Value or outcome-based
cells: Mostly to the firm[^7]
Needs an outcome you can measure

rules.name: NCEES Position Statement 6.10 on artificial intelligence
rules.what: Licensees keep responsible charge of AI-assisted work, validate the output and document their methods.[^8] Your state board decides what binds you.[^9]

rules.name: State engineering board AI guidance (North Carolina, Texas, North Dakota)
rules.status: Guidance; NC 16 Jul 2025, ND page dated 9 Nov 2026
rules.what: North Carolina says keep records and be able to reproduce AI output independently before you seal.[^9] Texas and North Dakota stress review, competence and client confidentiality.[^39][^40]

rules.name: National Society of Professional Engineers (NSPE), ethics case 24-2
rules.what: Putting client data into AI without permission, and leaving out citations, was found partly unethical.[^41] Get client consent before client data goes into an AI tool.

rules.name: AIA Code of Ethics, Rule 4.102
rules.what: Architects may sign and seal only documents prepared under their responsible control.[^10] Treat AI-made drawings and specs as work you must direct and check.

rules.name: Illinois Public Act 103-0804 (HB 3773)
rules.what: Employers must give notice when AI is used in hiring and other employment decisions, and may not use zip codes as a proxy.[^12] Staffing firms and any firm screening applicants are covered. Not legal advice.

rules.name: NYC Local Law 144, automated employment decision tools
rules.what: Before using an automated hiring tool for NYC jobs, get a bias audit within the past year and publish its summary.[^20] Candidates get notice 10 business days before use.[^20]

rules.name: California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) rules on automated decision tools
rules.status: Effective 1 Jan 2026; decision-tool duties from 1 Jan 2027
rules.what: Covered businesses using automated tools for significant decisions, including employment, owe pre-use notice, opt-out or appeal, and risk assessments.[^42] Not legal advice.

rules.name: Colorado SB 26-189
rules.what: Replaces the 2024 Colorado AI Act and covers automated tools used in consequential decisions, including hiring.[^43] Attorney General rules are still being written.[^43]

rules.name: Executive Order 14365
rules.what: Directs the Justice Department to challenge state AI laws.[^44] Until a court blocks one, plan to follow the state laws above.

rules.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC) rule on reviews and testimonials, 16 CFR 465
rules.what: Bans fake reviews and testimonials, including AI-written ones, with penalties up to $51,744 per violation (2024 figure).[^45] The FTC says there is no AI exemption from deception law.[^46]

rules.name: U.S. Copyright Office report on AI copyrightability
rules.what: Purely AI-generated material gets no copyright, but human selection, arrangement or changes to AI output can be protected.[^47] Agency and design deliverables need real human authorship to be owned.

watchOuts: Invented citations reached clients: an Australian government report was partly refunded, and Newfoundland and Labrador now requires AI-use disclosure in bids.[^13][^48][^18] Have a person check every source before delivery.
On a task outside AI's range, consultants using it were 19 points less likely to be right.[^14][^24] Test AI on your own past work before trusting it on a new kind of task.
Sloppy AI drafts pass the work to colleagues: 40% of US desk workers got one in a month, at about two hours each to fix.[^49][^50] Make the sender check the draft, not the receiver.

Client data in the wrong tool: an engineering ethics board found putting client data into AI without permission partly unethical.[^41][^39] Get client consent, and use a business plan with training switched off.

Saving time without capturing it: only 18% of legal, tax and risk professionals surveyed say their organization tracks AI return.[^3][^5] Set the pricing rule for saved hours before rollout, not after.

faq.q: Will AI cut our billable hours and revenue?
faq.a: Only on hourly work where saved hours aren't resold: by our math, one weekly hour per person risks $573,000-$700,000 of revenue at a 100-person firm.[^6] Professionals expect AI to free about five hours a week, which multiplies that.[^51] Fixed fees turn the same hours into margin.[^7]

faq.q: Are clients asking for AI discounts?
faq.a: Yes, some are: 42% of leaders at large firms say clients now question pricing.[^35]

faq.q: Do we have to tell clients we use AI?
faq.a: Not under any general US law we found, but contracts, engineering ethics and public bids can require it.[^41][^18] An engineering ethics board says get permission before client data goes into AI.[^41]

faq.q: Can an engineer seal AI-generated work?
faq.a: Only if the engineer kept responsible charge, checked the output and documented the method.[^8] North Carolina adds that the engineer must be able to reproduce it independently.[^9]

No study we found shows that; the evidence so far shows tasks changing, as one professional with AI matched a two-person team.[^28][^27] Keep juniors drafting some work themselves, so they still learn it.

faq.q: Which AI tools do mid-sized firms actually use?
faq.a: Mostly one general assistant plus the AI features inside tools they already own.[^15][^26] General plans list at $20-$25 a user a month, read 26 Nov 2026.[^36][^37]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy first: switch on the AI in your timesheet and proposal tools for one practice, then add one general assistant.[^36][^15][^52] Most companies buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases are bought, not built.[^53]
buyVsBuild.build: Build or connect only where a job crosses your systems, such as proposal library to customer database to billing.[^54][^27] MIT found partnered tools reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds, in a small sample.[^54]

pickElse: Your timesheet or project tool already has AI: turn on BigTime's AI Assistant or Productive's AI time tracking first (vendor features).[^15][^26]
Proposals are the bottleneck: dedicated RFP software such as Loopio ships generative AI in its base tier, priced by quote.[^52][^22]
Hourly contracts eat your savings: change the contract before the tool, moving suitable scopes to fixed fee.[^7][^16]
You only need a chat assistant with admin controls: a business plan such as ChatGPT Business, Copilot or Claude Team fits.[^36][^37]

sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Which unbilled hours should your firm hand AI first?
offer.body: Usually proposals or status reports; a free 30-minute call finds which one at your firm, from where your people's week goes. You leave with two or three jobs to start, which saved hours become margin under your contracts, and who reviews each output.

reviews.notes: Dana (COO): the title and bottom line answer 'what are firms like mine using AI for' in five lines, and every ranked job ends in a before-and-after measure. The human-role block names who checks and who owns the pricing call for saved hours, which is the decision a COO actually makes. Problem: NCEES, AIA, NSPE, FTC, CPPA and BEA appeared before being spelled out. Fixed: each is spelled out on first use. Every question heading opens with a direct answer sentence (answer gate: all answered first).

Ops head: wants to know what to switch on Monday and what changes for staff. The time-capture job only named one tool; fixed so it names Productive's calendar timesheets and BigTime's assistant, both labelled vendor features. The offer's first sentence read awkwardly; rewritten so it answers the heading plainly. Watch-outs each end in a control (source check, own-work test, sender checks the draft, client consent, pricing rule before rollout).

GM: wants cost and a way to trial it in one unit. Costs on the page are external and dated: ChatGPT Business, Copilot ($21 list, $18 offer to 31 Dec 2026) and Claude Team, read 26 Nov 2026; no Zavient price, per site rules. The own-data table turns a saved hour into dollars for his kind of firm, hourly versus fixed fee. Fixed: buy-or-build now says start with one practice before adding a general assistant.

Head of delivery / practice lead: wants evidence the quality holds and a clear review step. The jagged-frontier result (25.1% faster inside AI's range, 19 points worse outside it) and the Science writing study give peer-reviewed proof both ways. Problem: the code-drafting item cited the 2025 trial showing experienced developers slower without its authors' 2026 update. Fixed: the item now says the authors think developers are likely faster now. Knowledge search carries no payoff number, only what to measure, since none was sound.

Steve (managing partner, 40-500 staff): gets the answer in ten seconds from the bottom line, and the own-data number makes the billable-hour risk concrete for his firm type. 'Responsible charge' in the bottom line was jargon to him; fixed to 'keep the seal', with responsible charge explained lower down. His worries are covered: client data and consent, invented citations, clients asking for discounts, hiring-AI laws for his recruiters. Gap he will notice: no named case from a firm his size, because none had a citable page; none is claimed.
